[Resource from qmd at qmd://supabase/apps/docs/content/guides/database/connecting-to-postgres.mdx] 220: 
221: ```
222: Total backend load on Postgres =
223:  Direct connections +
224:  Supavisor backend connections (≤ supavisor_pool_size) +
225:  PgBouncer backend connections (≤ pgbouncer_pool_size)
226: ≤ Postgres max connections for your compute instance
227: ```
228: 
229: ### What is the max pooler clients limit?
230: 
231: The “max pooler clients” limit for your compute tier applies separately to Supavisor and PgBouncer. One pooler reaching its client limit does not affect the other. When a pooler reaches this limit, it stops accepting new client connections until existing ones are closed, but the other pooler remains unaffected. You can check your tier’s connection limits in the [compute and disk limits documentation](/docs/guides/platform/compute-and-disk#postgres-replication-slots-wal-senders-and-connections).
232: 
233: ### Where can you see current connection usage?
234: 
235: You can track connection usage from the [Observability](/dashboard/project/_/observability/database) section in your project dashboard. There are three key reports:
236: 
237: - **Database Connections:** shows total active connections by role (this includes direct and pooled connections).
238: - **Dedicated Pooler Client Connections:** shows the number of active client connections to PgBouncer.
239: - **Shared Pooler (Supavisor) Client Connections:** shows the number of active client connections to Supavisor.
240: 
241: Keep in mind that the Roles page is not real-time, it shows the connection count from the last refresh. If you need up-to-the-second data, set up Grafana or run the query against `pg_stat_activity` directly in SQL Editor. We have a few helpful queries for checking connections.
242: 
243: ```sql
244: -- Count connections by application and user name
245: select
246:   count(usename),
247:   count(application_name),
248:   application_name,
249:   usename
250: from
251:   pg_stat_ssl
252:   join pg_stat_activity on pg_stat_ssl.pid = pg_stat_activity.pid
253: group by usename, application_name;
254: ```
255: 
256: ```sql
257: -- View all connections
258:  SELECT
259:    pg_stat_activity.pid,

The other servers that communicate with Postgres (PostgREST, Realtime, and Auth) all rely on internal application poolers. 145: 146: Supavisor is primarily intended for users who do not want to rely on the Supabase Client libraries and instead prefer to work with external ORMs, such as Prisma, Drizzle, and Psycopg. 147: 148: ## **Whether to change Supavisor's pool size?** 149: 150: In an ideal scenario, Postgres would support an unlimited number of direct connections, but there's a limit to how many it can handle. If Supavisor uses most of the available connections, you risk depriving other servers, such as Auth, from accessing your database. Still, as much as possible, you want to give your pooler freedom to grow its pool as needed to service demand. 151: 152: It's important to note that the Storage server also uses Supavisor as a unique "user+db+mode" combination, so the pool size you set for your general application will apply to it, too. 153: 154: As a rule of thumb, if you're using the DB REST API or multiple app-based "user+db+mode" combinations, try to keep the pooler's usage under 40% of available connections. Otherwise, you can cautiously increase usage to around 80%. These percentages are flexible and depend on your application's usage and setup. Monitor connection usage to determine the optimal allocation without depriving other servers of necessary connections. 155: 156: ## **How to monitor connections** 157: 158: > EDIT: a more in-depth [troubleshooting guide](https://github.com/orgs/supabase/discussions/27141) for connection monitoring was published 159: 160: Connection usage can be monitored with a Supabase Grafana Dashboard. It provides realtime visibility of over 200 database metrics, such as graphs of CPU, EBS, and active direct/pooler connections. It can be extremely useful for monitoring and debugging instances. 161: 162: You can check our [GitHub repo](https://github.com/supabase/supabase-grafana) for setup instructions for local deployments or free cloud deployments on [Fly.io](http://fly.io/). content.text:
[Resource from qmd at qmd://supabase/apps/docs/content/troubleshooting/supavisor-faq-YyP5tI.mdx] 164: ## **Can Supavisor really support a million connections?**
165: 
166: It depends.
167: 
168: In the article ["Supavisor: Scaling Postgres to 1 Million Connections"](/blog/supavisor-1-million) we gave Supavisor the capacity to connect to a million clients simultaneously. The pooler triaged the clients' queries to 400 database connections.
169: 
170: What is important is that the database processing these queries had 64vCPUs and 256GB of memory. It could process the queries fast enough to ensure that there was never a noticeable bottleneck. The clients never waited long enough to timeout. If the clients were asking to run inefficient queries, like the one below, a severe backlog of pending client queries would have formed:
171: 
172: ```sql
173: -- do nothing for 60 seconds
174: select pg_sleep(60);
175: ```
176: 
177: A backlog could also happen if there are not enough direct connections available. In our setup, 400 connections were enough to handle a million clients, ensuring a smooth flow of requests. But if we had only 1 direct connection, the queue would've moved too slowly and clients would expire their requests.
178: 
179: Scaling to this level only works when the pooler is operating in transaction mode. In Session mode, hypothetically, the 400 clients that first accessed the direct connections could keep them, even if they are no longer executing queries. The pending 999,600 clients waiting for a turn would then be starved of direct connections.
180:

[Resource from qmd at qmd://supabase/apps/docs/content/guides/database/prisma/prisma-troubleshooting.mdx] 110: - **Baselining migrations**: [baselining](https://www.prisma.io/docs/orm/prisma-migrate/workflows/baselining) re-syncs Prisma by capturing the current database schema as the starting point for future migrations.
111: 
112: ---
113: 
114: ### Max client connections reached
115: 
116: Postgres or Supavisor rejected a request for more connections
117: 
118: #### Possible causes:[#possible-causes-max-client-connections-reached]
119: 
120: - **When working in transaction mode (port 6543):** The error "Max client connections reached" occurs when clients try to form more connections with the pooler than it can support.
121: - **When working in session mode (port 5432):** The max amount of clients is restricted to the "Pool Size" value in the [Database Settings](/dashboard/project/_/database/settings). If the "Pool Size" is set to 15, even if the pooler can handle 200 client connections, it will still be effectively capped at 15 for each unique ["database-role+database" combination](https://github.com/orgs/supabase/discussions/21566).
122: - **When working with direct connections**: Postgres is already servicing the max amount of connections
123: 
124: #### Solutions [#solutions-causes-max-client-connections-reached]
125: 
126: - **Transaction Mode for serverless apps**: If you are using serverless functions (Supabase Edge, Vercel, AWS Lambda), switch to transaction mode (port 6543). It handles more connections than session mode or direct connections.
127: - **Reduce the number of Prisma connections**: A single client-server can establish multiple connections with a pooler. Typically, serverless setups do not need many connections. Starting with fewer, like five or three, or even one, is often sufficient. In serverless setups, begin with `connection_limit=1`, increasing cautiously if needed to avoid maxing out connections.
128: - **Increase pool size**: If you are connecting with Supavisor, try increasing the pool size in the [Database Settings](/dashboard/project/_/database/settings).
129: - **Disconnect appropriately**: Close Prisma connections when they are no longer needed.
130: - **Decrease query time**: Reduce query complexity or add [strategic indexes](/docs/guides/database/postgres/indexes) to your tables to speed up queries.
131: - **Increase compute size**: Sometimes the best option is to increase your compute size, which also increases your max client size and query execution speed
132:

114: ### Max client connections reached
115: 
116: Postgres or Supavisor rejected a request for more connections
117: 
118: #### Possible causes:[#possible-causes-max-client-connections-reached]
119: 
120: - **When working in transaction mode (port 6543):** The error "Max client connections reached" occurs when clients try to form more connections with the pooler than it can support.
121: - **When working in session mode (port 5432):** The max amount of clients is restricted to the "Pool Size" value in the [Database Settings](/dashboard/project/_/database/settings). If the "Pool Size" is set to 15, even if the pooler can handle 200 client connections, it will still be effectively capped at 15 for each unique ["database-role+database" combination](https://github.com/orgs/supabase/discussions/21566).
122: - **When working with direct connections**: Postgres is already servicing the max amount of connections
123: 
124: #### Solutions [#solutions-causes-max-client-connections-reached]
125: 
126: - **Transaction Mode for serverless apps**: If you are using serverless functions (Supabase Edge, Vercel, AWS Lambda), switch to transaction mode (port 6543). It handles more connections than session mode or direct connections.
127: - **Reduce the number of Prisma connections**: A single client-server can establish multiple connections with a pooler. Typically, serverless setups do not need many connections. Starting with fewer, like five or three, or even one, is often sufficient. In serverless setups, begin with `connection_limit=1`, increasing cautiously if needed to avoid maxing out connections.
128: - **Increase pool size**: If you are connecting with Supavisor, try increasing the pool size in the [Database Settings](/dashboard/project/_/database/settings).
129: - **Disconnect appropriately**: Close Prisma connections when they are no longer needed.
130: - **Decrease query time**: Reduce query complexity or add [strategic indexes](/docs/guides/database/postgres/indexes) to your tables to speed up queries.
131: - **Increase compute size**: Sometimes the best option is to increase your compute size, which also increases your max client size and query execution speed

Yes — Supavisor has its own separate client-connection cap (per your compute tier's "max pooler clients" limit), plus a per-pool-size limit, independent of Postgres's `max_connections`.

- `connecting-to-postgres.mdx` (§"What is the max pooler clients limit?"): each compute tier has a max pooler clients limit for Supavisor, separate from PgBouncer/Postgres.
- `prisma-troubleshooting.mdx` (§"Max client connections reached"): in **transaction mode** (port 6543), the error fires when clients open more connections than the pooler can support; a sudden request surge is a classic trigger. Fix: use transaction mode, cap client connections (`connection_limit=1` or similar), disconnect promptly, or raise Supavisor's pool size / compute tier.
- `supavisor-faq-YyP5tI.mdx` (§"Can Supavisor really support a million connections?"): it *can* scale huge, but only if backend queries are fast enough that the queue doesn't back up — bursts of slow/many requests still exhaust it.

Since you open/close a connection per request (serverless-style) under bursty load, prefer transaction-mode pooling and consider reusing a small persistent pool instead of a new connection per request.
